# Script to clearance agent \- Workflow

**1\. Script-to-clearance agent — Parallel track**

Before a film can use a song, a brand logo, a painting on a wall, a real person's name, or a recognizable location, someone has to research who owns it and whether it's cleared. This work is real, expensive, done by paralegals and clearance coordinators, and it delays productions constantly.

Your agent ingests a screenplay PDF, extracts every clearable element — music cues, trademarks in dialogue or action lines, artworks, real people referenced, location names — then uses Parallel's Search API to research ownership, rights holders, public-domain status, and known litigation history for each one. Output is a clearance report with per-item risk ratings and cited sources.

**Why it scores:** This is unambiguously a media & entertainment workflow — it doesn't exist outside film and TV. Parallel's Search API isn't decorative here; research *is* the task, so partner fit is perfect. Potential Impact is easy to argue because the pain is well-documented. And it's non-obvious — nobody else will submit this.

**Why it's buildable:** Script parsing is a solved problem (the hackathon resources page even points at document processing and PDF parsing guides). The agent loop is extract → research → assess → report. No infrastructure, no simulation, no fake data anywhere.

**Risk:** Design. Your output is a document, so the product experience has to be a well-built review interface — script on one side, flagged items on the other, click to see sources and the agent's reasoning. Doable, but it's the whole frontend.

Tasks: 

1) Develop a web application  
2) Give option to upload the script  
3) In tokens: a full 120-page feature is roughly **30,000–40,000 tokens**. Set your upload cap at 25 MB and reject above it.

This is where a quarter of your score lives, so it's worth being opinionated. Let me show you the main screen, then work through the framework question.

### Framework

Next.js 15 with the App Router — but the reason isn't the usual one, and the usual one doesn't apply here.  
You have no SEO needs and no public content. This is a client-state-heavy dashboard behind an SSE connection, which is the exact profile where a plain Vite \+ React SPA is simpler and builds faster. Honestly it's close to a coin flip.  
What tips it: Next.js gives you API route proxying, so your browser calls /api/\* on the same origin and you never configure CORS. Over four weeks that's a real saving, and CORS misconfiguration is a classic day-before-demo failure. You also get a clean Cloud Run deployment story and file-based routing you don't have to think about.  
The trap to avoid: don't lean on React Server Components or server actions. Nearly every screen here is a client component driven by live state. Use the App Router for routing and mostly stay in "use client". Teams lose days fighting RSC boundaries on apps that never needed them.  
The supporting cast, kept deliberately short:

| Library | Why |
| ----- | ----- |
| Tailwind \+ shadcn/ui | Components without designing from scratch. shadcn is copy-in, so no version fights |
| TanStack Query | Server state, cache invalidation, and a polling fallback when SSE drops. Earns its place |
| TanStack Virtual | A 118-page script is thousands of DOM nodes. Virtualize the script pane |
| lucide-react | Icons, ships with shadcn |

Skip Redux and Zustand — TanStack Query holds server state and useState holds the rest. Skip a chart library; the risk counts are three numbers and a bar, which is CSS.  
Don't render the PDF. Render your parsed text styled as a screenplay — Courier, correct margins. Two reasons: you can only highlight char\_start/char\_end spans in text you control, and the rendered script is live proof your parser works. A PDF viewer proves nothing about your pipeline.

### Features, in build order

Tier 1 — the demo doesn't exist without these

1. Split-pane run view — script left, findings right. The screen in the mockup above is 90% of what a judge sees.  
2. Inline risk highlighting in the script text, colored by rating.  
3. Bidirectional linking — click a finding, the script scrolls and flashes the span; click a highlight, the finding opens. This is what makes it feel like a tool rather than a report generator.  
4. Progressive population. Critical, and I'd argue it's the single most important UX decision in the project: when a run starts, do *not* show a loading screen. Show the parsed script immediately and let findings drop into the right pane as SSE events arrive. The user watches the analysis happen.  
5. Live agent feed — the strip at the bottom showing actual search queries as they run. Twenty seconds of that in your video does more than any architecture slide.  
6. Finding detail panel — full rationale, sources with excerpts, the queries the agent ran, suggested alternatives.

Tier 2 — where Design points actually accumulate

7. Accept / override with a note. Judges reward a visible human-in-the-loop path, and it's the honest posture for legal-adjacent work.  
8. Filters — risk, category, review status, scene range.  
9. Risk summary header with counts, always visible.  
10. Upload flow with a dropzone, parse progress, and clear rejection for scanned PDFs.  
11. Report export.

Tier 3 — only after Aug 29

12. Re-run and diff view. 13\. Scene navigator. 14\. Keyboard shortcuts (j/k through findings — cheap, and it reads as a tool built for someone who uses it all day).

### Four design principles

Color means risk and nothing else. No brand color, no decorative accents, no colored buttons. When the only color on screen is red, amber, and green, the eye goes straight to the nine RED findings. Introduce a purple logo and you've diluted your own signal.  
Monospace for script, sans for chrome. The script pane should look like a screenplay — Courier, screenplay margins, the character name indented. Everything around it is your UI font. That contrast makes the app instantly legible and quietly signals you know the format.  
Dense, not sparse. The reference points are Linear and Notion, not a marketing landing page. Your user is a clearance coordinator working through 84 findings. Small type, tight rows, lots of information visible at once. Hackathon projects usually fail by being too airy and empty.  
Never a full-screen spinner. Every waiting state should show something real — parsed script, findings so far, the current search query. This is both better UX and the difference between a video where something is happening and a video where a progress bar moves.  
Want me to build the run view as actual React next, or write the rubric? The rubric is still the one undefined piece that determines whether any of this displays good content.

Here are the ones that will actually come up, with what I'd recommend.

### **1\. The judge who opens your URL has no screenplay**

This is the highest-value one and it's routinely missed. A judge clicks your hosted link, sees an empty dropzone, and has nothing to upload. They bounce in ten seconds.

Ship a **preloaded demo script with a completed run** as the landing state. They land directly in the review view with 84 findings already there, and "upload your own" is secondary. Make the demo run instantly re-playable so they can watch the agent work without waiting four minutes.

### **2\. Group by element, not by mention**

You'll have \~84 findings but only \~40 distinct things. Twelve Coca-Cola mentions shouldn't be twelve rows.

Group by canonical element, expandable to its mentions. A producer thinks "we have a Coca-Cola problem," not "we have twelve Coca-Cola problems." The exception is when mentions rate differently — Take On Me is RED in action and GREEN in dialogue, so that one splits, and the split is the interesting part.

### **3\. Failed research must be loud, not hidden**

Some elements will fail — Parallel returns nothing useful, or the agent hits its step cap. The tempting thing is to drop them.

Don't. A **fourth state — "unresearched, needs manual review"** — pinned to the top of the list, above RED. A clearance report that silently omits four items is worse than useless; it's dangerous, because the production believes it's covered. Surfacing failures is what makes the tool trustworthy, and it's a maturity signal a judge will notice.

### **4\. Confidence: three states, not a number**

Don't show `0.72`. Users can't calibrate a decimal and it makes everything feel shaky.

Show **"confirmed" / "verify" / "uncertain"**, derived from source count and agreement. Sort uncertain items up rather than hiding them — never suppress a finding for low confidence in a tool whose purpose is catching things.

### **5\. Review completion turns a report into a workflow**

Add a "31 of 84 reviewed" counter and a per-finding reviewed state. It reframes the product from "here's a document" to "here's a task you can finish," which is what a clearance coordinator actually needs. It's also nearly free once accept/override exists.

### **6\. Default ordering, and what the agent processes first**

Findings default to risk descending, then scene order — with a toggle for pure script order, since a coordinator reads linearly.

Separately: have the **agent process in scene order**, not by category. Findings then appear in the same sequence as the script the user is reading, which makes the live population feel coherent rather than random. Costs nothing, feels much better.

### **7\. Make the export look like a real clearance report**

Your PDF export is the artifact that would go to the insurer. Mirroring the conventional shape — cover page with counts, findings grouped by category, each with scene, page, rights required, rightsholders, sources — costs an afternoon and buys real credibility. It's the difference between a demo and a thing.

### **8\. The impact number, stated once and carefully**

Somewhere in the UI: this run took six minutes; the manual equivalent is five to ten business days and a few thousand dollars. That's your Potential Impact criterion in one line.

Put it in the report header, stated flatly. Don't put a "saved you $3,400\!" banner in the app — that reads as a pitch deck and undercuts the professional tone everything else is doing.

### **9\. Give it a name**

"Script-to-clearance agent" is a description. A name changes how the whole thing reads, and it costs you fifteen minutes. Aim for something in the register of production tooling rather than AI branding.

### **10\. Two things to explicitly not decide**

**Dark mode** — skip it. Zero score, real hours.

**Mobile responsive** — skip the work, but do check the app doesn't visibly collapse at narrow widths, because a judge may open your link on a phone. A `min-width` with horizontal scroll is an acceptable answer.

---

Of these, **\#1 and \#3** are the two I'd treat as non-negotiable. The demo landing state determines whether a judge sees your work at all, and the failure-state handling is the clearest signal in the whole product that you understood what you were building rather than just building it.

# Workload breakdown

Here's the full breakdown. Twenty-seven units, grouped into five blocks, ordered by dependency. Each one has a clear finish line so you always know whether it's done.

### **Block A — Foundations (Aug 10–11)**

| \# | Unit | Done when | Effort |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| A1 | Repo, `.env`, compose stack | `docker compose up` → all three services healthy, `/docs` loads | ½ day |
| A2 | **Probe scripts** — bare Parallel \+ Gemini calls | Both print real responses. No framework, no Docker | ½ day |
| A3 | Schema \+ SQLAlchemy models \+ Alembic | Tables exist, models round-trip a row | ½ day |

A2 is the one that matters. You're designing every contract downstream around Parallel's actual response shape, so you need to see it before anything else.

### **Block B — Parser (Aug 12–15) · no AI at all**

| \# | Unit | Done when | Effort |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| B1 | Upload endpoint | 25MB cap, magic-byte check, SHA-256 de-dupe, file in storage, `scripts` row | ½ day |
| B2 | Page text \+ word coordinates | `pdfplumber` returns words with x/y per page | ½ day |
| B3 | Text-layer detection | Scanned PDF rejected with `NO_TEXT_LAYER` | 1 hr |
| B4 | Element classification by x-position | Every line typed: action, character, dialogue, parenthetical, transition | 1 day |
| B5 | Scene grouping | Slug detection, mini-slug rejection, margin scene numbers stripped, page furniture dropped | 1 day |
| B6 | Persist \+ read endpoints | `GET /scripts/{id}/scenes` returns the parsed structure | ½ day |
| B7 | **Your test screenplay** | 10 pages, planted elements with known answers | 2 hrs |

B4 and B5 are the fiddliest code in the project and they block everything. B7 looks like a detour and is the thing that makes your rubric tunable.

### **Block C — Agent (Aug 16–22)**

| \# | Unit | Done when | Effort |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| C1 | Extraction agent, one chunk | Structured elements from one scene group, Pydantic-validated | 1 day |
| C2 | Chunking \+ full-script extraction | 8–10 scene chunks, all persisted to `elements` | ½ day |
| C3 | Canonicalization \+ dedup | 12 Coca-Cola mentions → 1 research task | ½ day |
| C4 | Parallel tool wrapper | ADK tool: query in, normalized results out, errors handled | ½ day |
| C5 | Research agent | Loop with 6-call cap, evidence dossier out, cache read/write | 1½ days |
| C6 | **Rubric \+ assessment agent** | Batched \~10, per-mention ratings, cites only dossier evidence | 2 days |
| C7 | ADK workflow wiring | `SequentialAgent` \+ `ParallelAgent`, concurrency capped 5–8 | 1 day |
| C8 | Run orchestration | Background task, status transitions, partial-failure handling | 1 day |
| C9 | Event bus \+ SSE endpoint | Snapshot-on-connect, then live events | ½ day |

C6 is the highest-leverage unit in the project. Two days is not padding.

### **Block D — Frontend (Aug 23–29)**

| \# | Unit | Done when | Effort |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| D1 | Shell, routing, API client, TanStack Query | Upload screen works against the real API | ½ day |
| D2 | Script pane | Screenplay-styled render, virtualized, scroll-to-page | 1 day |
| D3 | Findings pane \+ filters | Grouped by element, risk/category/review filters | 1 day |
| D4 | Bidirectional linking | Click finding → script scrolls and flashes span; click span → finding opens | ½ day |
| D5 | Live run consumption | SSE → progressive population, never a full-screen spinner | 1 day |
| D6 | Finding detail panel | Rationale, sources, `queries_run`, alternatives | ½ day |
| D7 | Accept / override | `PATCH`, optimistic update, review counter | ½ day |
| D8 | Summary header \+ demo landing state | Counts always visible; judge lands on a completed run | ½ day |

D8's landing state is small and disproportionately important — it decides whether a judge sees your work at all.

### **Block E — Delivery (Aug 30 – Sep 6\)**

| \# | Unit | Done when |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| E1 | Report export | PDF shaped like a real clearance report |
| E2 | Production build \+ Cloud Run \+ Secret Manager | Hosted URL works from a phone on cellular |
| E3 | Demo data seeded, demo run pre-computed | Instant replay, no live gamble |
| E4 | Video, README, Devpost submission | Submitted Sep 5–6 |

---

### **Splitting it**

Person A takes B and C. Person B takes A1, then D — building against a **stubbed API contract from day one** so they never wait on the agent. Agree the response shapes in writing on Aug 11; that seam is where two-person projects lose days.

Both do E.

### **Critical path**

`A2 → B4 → B5 → C1 → C5 → C6 → C7`. Everything else can slip a day without hurting. If any of those slips two days, cut a D-block unit rather than compressing C6.

# Backend Design

**Python 3.12 \+ FastAPI**, with the agent running in-process.

The full backend stack:

| Layer | Choice |
| ----- | ----- |
| Language | Python 3.12 |
| Web framework | FastAPI \+ uvicorn |
| Agent framework | Google ADK (`google-adk`, `google-cloud-aiplatform`) |
| Models | Gemini Flash (extraction, research) \+ Pro (assessment) |
| Search | Parallel Search via `parallel-web` |
| Validation | Pydantic v2 |
| ORM | SQLAlchemy 2 async \+ asyncpg |
| Database | Postgres 16 |
| PDF | pdfplumber |
| Streaming | sse-starlette |
| Packaging | uv |

### **Why Python isn't really a choice**

ADK is Python-first, and the hackathon's accepted SDK list — `google-adk`, `google-genai`, `google-generativeai`, `google-cloud-aiplatform` — is where the ecosystem lives. There's a TypeScript path (`parallel-web` ships a TS SDK, and ADK has JS support), but it's the less-trodden route with thinner docs, and you'd be discovering gaps under a four-week deadline. Not the place to be adventurous.

Given Python for the agent, putting the API in a second language would mean two runtimes, two dependency systems, and an HTTP hop between your endpoint and your agent. FastAPI keeps it to one process.

### **Why FastAPI specifically**

Three things line up unusually well here:

**Pydantic is already your stage contracts.** Every agent boundary — extraction output, research dossier, assessment result — is a Pydantic model. FastAPI uses those same models for request/response validation and generates OpenAPI docs from them for free. One schema definition serves the model output, the database write, and the API response.

**Async matches the workload.** Everything is IO-bound: Gemini calls, Parallel searches, Postgres. `asyncio` handles the fan-out across 40 concurrent research tasks without threads.

**Background tasks are built in.** `POST /runs` returns `202` and the agent runs in the same process. No Celery, no broker.

### **The one thing to be deliberate about**

**Single uvicorn worker.** The agent streams progress through an in-memory event bus, and multiple workers would split that bus across processes so some SSE clients silently get nothing.

That's a real limitation and you should name it rather than hide it: production would move the agent to Cloud Tasks or Pub/Sub with separate workers, for retries and backpressure as much as for scale. Saying "here's the constraint we accepted and why" reads as engineering judgement; a judge who's run infrastructure will ask, and having the answer ready is worth more than pretending the problem doesn't exist.
